newsitem.title: USA: Calif. utilities board reviews electric metering.
newsitem.headline: Calif. utilities board reviews electric metering.

text.p: The California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) heard comments today on the issue of real-time electricity metering during the morning session of a forum on direct access.
With the state set to begin open access for some electricity consumers in January 1998, the commissioners sought direction on how cost signals can be communicated to end-users.

Currently, most consumers are billed based on flat rates as opposed to time-of-use. Access to information on underlying costs could, for instance, lead consumers to shift some power usage to off-peak hours when prices are lower.
"Any scheme that encourages ignorance of underlying costs is the wrong scheme," noted commissioner Daniel Fessler during the San Francisco forum.
John Fielder, an executive with Edison International's Southern California Edison Co, said metering will be "part and parcel" of the utility's future role as a distribution business.
He explained that technology is moving in the right direction, but it will probably be two to five years before technology enabling economies of scale for metering would be available.
As an interim step, Edison proposed "load-profiling" as a means for residential customers to benefit from deregulation.
Load profiling would set rates based on time-of-use for bulk classes of customers, such as small commercial or residential.
But CPUC president Gregory Conlon questioned whether load profiling would give customers, especially those located in high-use climates such as Palm Springs, enough choices.
Commissioner Josiah Neeper, however, said he thought open access meant that regulators would get out of the electricity business and let competition work toward the social good.
A representative from a metering company pointed out that users would miss out on the economies of scale associated with metering if it were not implemented at the regulatory level.
A representative from the CPUC's Division of Ratepayer Advocates suggested that the commission "incent but not mandate metering."
